title: A solid-state battery: OSO vs. traditional research
html:
A solid-state battery: OSO vs. traditional research

Twenty ideas from electrolyte chemistry to a working cell, written out by hand; two bounties.

For the same money, the OSO community got further, or got there more cheaply, than the traditional one.

  • How far: with a budget of 240 money, OSO reached level 5.0 of 5 on average; traditional research reached 2.0.
  • Targets solved: OSO solved 1.9 of 2; traditional solved 0.6.
  • Cost to reach level 5: OSO 136 money (in the 95% of runs that got there); traditional 222 money (in the 9% of runs that got there).
  • Return on the money (ROI): OSO gained 3.70 in bounty value per unit spent (472 for 144); traditional 0.37 (85 for 235). Value gained is the bounties of the targets solved.
  • Does flow-back make agents share? When agents choose, sharing rises clearly (by 0.2 or more) once α is 0.5 or lower. At OSO's default α = 0.8, agents shared 18% of their intermediate ideas.
  • Robustness: OSO's lead in level is smallest when shared knowledge is costly to take up (+2.5 levels).
  • Sensitivity: Across the tested values of the parameters a market or community sets, OSO's lead (agents choosing what to share) runs from +0.1 to +3.0 levels. The smallest lead, at ρ, money follows earnings = 100%, is within noise: no clear difference there. The lead is most sensitive to ρ, money follows earnings. Why ρ matters so much here: under traditional rules, when money follows earnings, the first agent to earn takes the money. In this community that is the gaming agent, which earns early from trivial ideas and then, holding all the money, does the research too. Without a gaming agent the effect disappears (see the funding-rule-gamer experiment).

The verdict compares the hardest level reached, the targets solved and (when both communities reach level 5 in at least 90% of runs) the cost to get there, each against two standard errors. 100 simulated runs per setting · simulator commit 4bd670b+ · 2026-10-23. This is a simulation with guessed parameters, not evidence about real research; see What this shows.

1. The problem space

Building a solid-state lithium battery. Three lines of work run in parallel: the solid electrolyte (finding a conducting material, making it stable and making it thin), the interfaces (stopping dendrites and keeping contact as the cell breathes), and manufacturing (making layers at scale). A working laboratory cell needs ideas from all three; a cell that survives a thousand cycles needs more. Some promising lines (a polymer electrolyte, a coating that never scales) lead nowhere.

In this space means
an idea a demonstrated material property or process step
a target a cell that meets a performance milestone
an attempt one round of synthesis and testing
an area a line of work
an agent a lab or startup

The tree has 20 ideas in 5 levels and 3 areas (electrolyte, interfaces, manufacturing). 6 are dead ends: no target depends on them. 2 are targets:

target level bounty ideas it rests on
lab-cell 4 100 9
thousand-cycle-cell 5 400 13

How hard each level is, before an agent's skill:

level results targets success chance per attempt
1 5 0 50%
2 5 0 20%

4 3 1 6%

The community has 12 agents (3 foundation, 3 racer, 2 explorer, 2 specialist, 1 freeRider, 1 gamer) and a budget of 240 money over 20 rounds (calibrated: the smallest budget at which OSO solves about 90% of the targets).

2. Progress for the money

Each line is the mean, over 100 runs, of the hardest level the community had published after spending that much money. A line that ends early means every target was solved and the funder stopped paying.

3. The six settings

The rules are the only difference between rows (specification, section 3). Traditional: nothing flows back to what an idea built on, and work is published only when finished. OSO: value flows back (α = 0.8, c = 0.15), and ideas are published at once or when the agent chooses.

Sharing rises clearly once α is 0.5 or lower: this is the threshold α* in this space. The threshold depends on the scoop risk ψ = 0.5, which is a guess.

5. When sharing is costly or sometimes wrong

Taking up a published idea costs 0.5; proofs are wrong 10% of the time, ideas built on a wrong idea are wrong too, and targets reveal and retract them.

shared knowledge traditional frontier OSO frontier OSO lead traditional targets OSO targets
free and correct 2.0 5.0 +2.9 0.6 1.9
costly to take up 2.0 4.5 +2.5 0.6 1.4
sometimes wrong 0.8 4.6 +3.9 0.2 1.5
costly and sometimes wrong 0.7 4.2 +3.5 0.2 0.9

6. Sensitivity to the parameters

In OSO, α and c are set by each community (OIP-14), validators decide how strict the screen is, funders decide how far money follows earnings, and the mint may become a community parameter (OIP-8). Their values will be set by competing communities, not by us, so the result must hold across them. The parameters below the line are our guesses about how agents think.

Each parameter is varied alone, from this space's settings, with agents choosing what to share (the realistic case: incentives matter only if sharing is a choice). The lead is OSO's hardest level reached minus traditional's under the same parameter value; α and c do not exist under traditional rules, so there it is compared with traditional's default.

Across the tested values of the parameters a market or community sets, OSO's lead (agents choosing what to share) runs from +0.1 to +3.0 levels. The smallest lead, at ρ, money follows earnings = 100%, is within noise: no clear difference there. The lead is most sensitive to ρ, money follows earnings. Why ρ matters so much here: under traditional rules, when money follows earnings, the first agent to earn takes the money. In this community that is the gaming agent, which earns early from trivial ideas and then, holding all the money, does the research too. Without a gaming agent the effect disappears (see the funding-rule-gamer experiment).

What this shows and what it does not

  • It is a simulation of the OSO demo specification: ideas are abstract, success is chance, and agents follow a formula. It shows how the incentive rules play out if this space works as described, not that it does.
  • The parameters are guesses, especially the success chances, the scoop risk ψ, and the costs and error rates in section 5. Section 6 varies each one alone; it does not vary them together, except α and c.
  • By default, sharing is free and always correct, which favours OSO; section 5 shows how much of the lead survives without that.
  • Notes for this space: The structure is a simplified sketch, and the success chances follow the default model by level; neither is from the battery literature.

Reproduce

npm run sim -- report solid-state-battery --seeds 100

The space is spaces/solid-state-battery.yaml (written by hand as an example of a space listed idea by idea (the graph world)). Every number above is in data.json. Generated by the OSO simulator at commit 4bd670b+ (with uncommitted changes).
